rows.grounds: the speaker too is a suitable means
one who knows that teaching also
a fellow disciple of the teacher

items.question: Who can serve as a suitable means for transmitting this knowledge?
premises: The scripture is a means for attaining that knowledge.
A suitable speaker, namely the teacher, is also a means.
One who knows that teaching, such as a fellow disciple, can give knowledge through dialogue.
items.inference: Knowledge can be transmitted through scripture, the teacher, or a knowledgeable fellow disciple in dialogue.
uncertainties: The exact scope of 'tad' (that) depends on the immediately preceding discussion of knowledge.
items.plain_english: Here the means is the scripture, and a suitable speaker is the teacher. Even one who knows that teaching, such as a fellow disciple, can give knowledge through dialogue.

rows.grounds: their status arises from connection through knowledge, not birth

items.question: What makes the teacher's family and associates part of the teacher's group?
premises: The teacher's wife, brother, son, and others form a group around the teacher.
This group is not constituted by birth connection.
This group is constituted by connection through knowledge.
items.inference: Membership in the teacher's group depends on a bond of knowledge rather than a bond of birth.
uncertainties: The verse states the principle generally and does not specify whether every family member automatically shares that knowledge bond.
items.plain_english: The teacher's wife, brother, son, and others may be called the teacher's group, but not because of birth ties. They belong to that group because of their connection through knowledge.

rows.grounds: established in body and ego formed from seed and menstrual blood
a lineage that supports the body

items.question: How are blood relatives characterized in relation to bodily lineage?
premises: Blood relatives are established in body and ego formed from seed and menstrual blood.
They form a lineage that supports the body.
Their kinship is fully established in that bodily basis.
items.inference: Blood kinship is grounded in bodily origin and bodily continuity.
uncertainties: The compound is dense, and the exact nuance of 'ahantā' here may range from ego-sense to personal identity.
items.plain_english: Blood relatives are rooted in a body and sense of self that come from seed and blood. They form a lineage that supports the body, and their kinship is firmly established on that basis.

rows.grounds: in the texts of traditional law
the taking of inheritance by lineage
according to degrees of nearness and distance

items.question: Why is inheritance by bodily lineage considered appropriate in traditional law?
premises: Traditional law texts assign inheritance through lineage.
Such inheritance is fitting because it follows bodily kinship.
The strength of that claim varies with nearness and distance within the lineage.
items.inference: Inheritance rules in traditional law reflect graded degrees of bodily kinship.
uncertainties: The verse compresses a legal argument, so the exact procedural details of inheritance are not spelled out.
items.plain_english: So in the traditional law texts, it is fitting that inheritance goes through lineage. That claim is appropriate to the degree of nearness or distance within the family.

rows.grounds: have given up attachment to the body
share in awareness and the sense of 'I'
they belong through two lineages that support awareness

items.question: What kind of kinship belongs to those who have moved beyond bodily attachment?
premises: Some people abandon attachment to the body.
They share in awareness and the sense of 'I'.
They are connected through two lineages that support awareness.
items.inference: A higher kinship can be based on shared awareness rather than bodily descent.
uncertainties: The phrase 'two lineages that support awareness' is not fully explained in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: But those who have let go of attachment to the body share in awareness and the sense of 'I'. Through two lineages that support awareness, they enjoy a true kinship.

rows.grounds: in that context, in this way
when one looks back to earlier stages
with seeing and acting opened by the Lord's power
formed from earlier and earlier material causes

items.question: How should one understand the formation of the body when viewed in this way?
premises: One may look back with seeing and acting opened by the Lord's power.
From that perspective, this body is seen as produced.
Its production traces back through earlier and earlier material causes.
items.inference: The body appears as a product of a long causal chain when seen from an awakened perspective.
uncertainties: The verse introduces a contemplative perspective, but it does not yet state the full metaphysical conclusion.
items.plain_english: In that context, when one looks with vision and action opened by the Lord's power, this body is seen to be formed from earlier and earlier material causes.

rows.grounds: without a cause because it is eternal
again, from its own nature, this appears

items.question: If the self is changeless and eternal, how can it appear in embodied form?
premises: The self is free from change.
Because it is eternal, it has no cause.
Through its own freedom, it appears as if concealed in its own embodied condition.
items.inference: Embodiment does not alter the self but appears as a concealment arising from the self's freedom.
uncertainties: The phrase 'punarātmīyāt' is compact and could also be read with a slightly different causal nuance.
items.plain_english: The self is changeless and, because it is eternal, without a cause. Yet through its own freedom it seems to stand concealed, as if taking on its own embodied condition.

rows.grounds: becomes fit for the state of Bhairava

items.question: What happens when the self becomes manifest again?
premises: The self can become manifest again.
In that manifestation it becomes fit for the state of Bhairava.
That manifestation strongly involves both enjoyment and liberation.
items.inference: The self's re-manifestation culminates in the Bhairava state, which encompasses enjoyment and liberation.
uncertainties: The verse ends abruptly in sense and is completed by the next verse's discussion of the means.
items.plain_english: And again, when it becomes manifest, it becomes fit for the state of Bhairava. In that manifestation, which consists greatly of both enjoyment and liberation,

rows.grounds: through a stream of such and similar knowledge gradually becoming clear

items.question: What is the suitable means for that manifestation of the Bhairava state?
premises: A suitable means is required for that manifestation.
That means is the lineage of knowledge.
It works through a gradually clarifying stream of such and similar knowledge.
items.inference: The knowledge lineage is the effective means because it steadily clarifies the relevant realization.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'such and similar knowledge' depends on the preceding account of manifestation.
items.plain_english: The suitable means for that is the lineage of knowledge. It works through a stream of such and similar knowledge that gradually becomes clear.

rows.grounds: and of a knowledge lineage accustomed to beginningless worldly life

items.question: How does the knowledge lineage make the goal attainable quickly?
premises: As otherness fades, the goal becomes accessible.
What is to be attained is then obtained quickly.
This matters especially for a knowledge lineage long accustomed to beginningless worldly life.
items.inference: The fading of otherness within the knowledge lineage accelerates attainment, even against long worldly conditioning.
uncertainties: The genitive at the end sets up the next verse, so its full syntactic role is completed there.
items.plain_english: As otherness fades away, what is to be attained is indeed obtained quickly. This is especially relevant for a knowledge lineage long accustomed to beginningless worldly life.

rows.grounds: would take on or resort to
of a noble knowledge lineage not accustomed to worldly life

items.question: What happens when a worldly knowledge lineage is destroyed?
premises: A knowledge lineage accustomed to beginningless worldly life can be destroyed.
When it is destroyed, transcendent knowledge can take the place of another lineage.
That other lineage is a noble knowledge lineage not accustomed to worldly life.
items.inference: The destruction of worldly conditioning allows one to enter a transcendent knowledge lineage.
uncertainties: The optative 'śrayet' may express a general principle or a hypothetical transition.
items.plain_english: When that worldly knowledge lineage is destroyed, transcendent knowledge would take on the character of another lineage, namely a noble knowledge lineage not accustomed to worldly life.

rows.grounds: that knowledge of the teacher entering the self

items.question: What is the primary cause of entry into that noble knowledge lineage?
premises: A primary and original cause is identified.
That cause is the teacher's knowledge entering the disciple's self.
It works by clearly bestowing its own special qualities.
items.inference: The teacher's transmitted knowledge is the chief cause of transformation into the noble knowledge lineage.
uncertainties: The verse emphasizes transmission but does not detail the ritual or pedagogical mechanism.
items.plain_english: The primary and original cause is the teacher's knowledge entering the self. It works clearly by bestowing its own special qualities there.

items.question: How do bodily difference and knowledge continuity relate to each other?
premises: The teacher's knowledge functions as a fitting material basis.
Bodies may differ even when there is continuity.
Difference and non-difference in the bodily lineage do not determine the knowledge lineage in the same way.
items.inference: The continuity of the knowledge lineage is not governed by bodily sameness or difference.
uncertainties: The syntax is compressed; the contrast between bodily and knowledge lineage is inferred from the argument's flow.
items.plain_english: That knowledge is a fitting material basis. Even when bodies differ, the difference and non-difference that belong to the bodily lineage do not apply in the same way to the lineage of knowledge.

rows.grounds: for being of that same kind
like a corpse body entered by a yogi's will
in causing life in another body and so on

items.question: Does a yogi's animation of another body create the same kind of knowledge lineage?
premises: A yogi may enter and animate another body by will.
Such a case is compared to a corpse body entered by a yogi.
This does not establish the same kind of knowledge-lineage continuity.
items.inference: Animating another body is not equivalent to transmitting a knowledge lineage.
uncertainties: The verse is elliptical and relies on the following verse to complete the argument.
items.plain_english: It is not the same as that, like a corpse body entered by a yogi's will. When a yogi causes life in another body and so on, while keeping his own,

rows.grounds: the state of being a material basis for various knowledges
because the knowledge lineage is primary over the bodily lineage

items.question: Why does the yogi's case not undermine the primacy of the knowledge lineage?
premises: A yogi may act on other bodies without abandoning his own.
This does not make him the material basis of various knowledge lineages in the same way.
The knowledge lineage is primary over the bodily lineage.
items.inference: Extraordinary bodily influence does not override the primacy of transmitted knowledge.
uncertainties: The rhetorical 'na kim' is read as an emphatic affirmation in context.
items.plain_english: Even while not abandoning his own body, he does not thereby become the material basis for various knowledge lineages. Therefore, the knowledge lineage is primary over the bodily lineage.

items.question: How is the teacher lineage structured when it is grounded in Shiva knowledge?
premises: The teacher lineage is mutually connected.
It is established in knowledge of Shiva.
When so established, it involves a primary cause and an assisting cause in a threefold structure.
items.inference: The teacher lineage functions through an ordered structure of primary and assisting causes grounded in Shiva knowledge.
uncertainties: The exact threefold division is clarified in the next verse.
items.plain_english: The teacher lineage, mutually connected and established in knowledge of Shiva, stands in this way as a threefold structure with a primary cause and an assisting cause.

rows.grounds: sharing one cause and one effect
is here said to be the cause

items.question: How are the teacher and his wife positioned within the teacher's group?
premises: The teacher's group is described as sharing one cause and one effect.
The teacher is identified as the cause.
The teacher's wife is identified as the assisting cause.
items.inference: Within the teacher's group, the teacher is the primary cause and his wife functions as the assisting cause.
uncertainties: The verse names only two roles explicitly, while verse 208 suggested a threefold structure.
items.plain_english: Thus the teacher's group is a single reality sharing one cause and one effect. Here the teacher is said to be the cause, and his wife is the assisting cause.

rows.grounds: there would be no eligibility in the rite
of the inner noble awareness-power, the outer

items.question: Why is the teacher's wife described as an assisting cause in ritual eligibility?
premises: Without power, one would lack eligibility in the rite.
The teacher's wife is associated with an outer form of power.
The verse contrasts this with inner noble awareness-power.
items.inference: The assisting role is explained through the need for power in ritual eligibility, with an outer power complementing inner awareness.
uncertainties: The syntax is compressed and the sentence continues into the next verse, so the full comparison is completed there.
items.plain_english: Because without power there would be no eligibility in the rite, the outer power is considered in relation to the inner noble power of awareness, even without that outer form.

rows.grounds: they would be so, and whoever is similar to that

items.question: How does the analogy of the yogi clarify the roles of assisting causes and brothers in the lineage?
premises: A yogi may have capacity even without an assisting cause.
Brothers are described as born of one source.
Anyone similar to that shared-source relation can be counted in the same way.
items.inference: The lineage can include both exceptional independence and relations defined by shared origin or similarity.
uncertainties: The verse is highly compressed, and the exact mapping of 'brothers' to the earlier threefold structure is interpretive.
items.plain_english: Just as a yogi can have capacity even without an assisting cause, brothers are those born of one source; and anyone similar to that may also be counted in that way.

rows.grounds: the teacher group also, by connection through lineage

items.question: Why should the teacher lineage be honored at all times?
premises: The teacher group is also understood through lineage connection.
This lineage is identified as primary.
What is primary in this transmission deserves worship and honor.
items.inference: Because the teacher lineage is primary in transmission, it should always be worshiped and honored.
uncertainties: The verse states the duty of honor but does not specify the ritual forms it takes.
items.plain_english: Again, by connection through lineage, this is also called the teacher group. But this primary lineage should always be worshiped and honored.

rows.grounds: a cause of knowledge, means, body, and so on

items.question: Why are the birth, initiation, and death days of teachers ritually significant?
premises: Teachers and others have significant days of birth, initiation, and death.
Each of these days marks a causal moment.
That causal moment concerns knowledge, means, body, and related factors.
items.inference: These days are significant because they mark causal junctures in the transmission of knowledge and embodied life.
uncertainties: The verse states the principle broadly and leaves the specific observances to be inferred from context.
items.plain_english: For teachers and others, the days of birth, initiation, and death are significant, because each such day is a cause connected with knowledge, the means, the body, and so on.

rows.grounds: of the body that is the cause of such enjoyment, liberation, and so on

items.question: In what sense can one's own birth day be called a means of knowledge?
premises: One's own birth day is called a means of knowledge.
It is connected with the body that makes possible such enjoyment and liberation.
That bodily occasion functions as a cause in the larger spiritual process.
items.inference: One's birth day is ritually meaningful because it marks the bodily condition for knowledge, enjoyment, and liberation.
uncertainties: The verse links bodily birth to knowledge indirectly, through the body's role in spiritual attainment.
items.plain_english: In this way, one's own birth day is called a means of knowledge, because it is connected with the body that becomes a cause of such enjoyment, liberation, and so on.

rows.grounds: because of birth in the knowledge lineage

items.question: Why can the day of initiation be considered a primary birth day?
premises: Initiation and related consecrations transform one's own self.
The day on which such a consecration occurs marks a new beginning.
That beginning is a birth within the knowledge lineage.
items.inference: The day of initiation counts as a primary birth day because it marks birth into the knowledge lineage.
uncertainties: The verse treats initiation as paradigmatic; other consecrations are included but not individually specified.
items.plain_english: And when initiation or another consecration of one's own self takes place, that day becomes a primary birth day, because it is a birth in the lineage of knowledge.

rows.grounds: because at that time he is non-different from Shiva

items.question: Why is one's own death day treated as an occasional observance for others rather than for oneself?
premises: One's own death day is considered in relation to others.
For others it becomes an occasional observance.
At death, the person is non-different from Shiva.
items.inference: The death day is ritually marked by others because the deceased is understood to be non-different from Shiva.
uncertainties: The verse assumes the theological claim of non-difference from Shiva rather than arguing for it here.
items.plain_english: One's own death day will be an occasional observance for others, because at that time the one who has died would be non-different from Shiva.
